WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Listen closely and you'll hear squeals of disgust from a watchdog group tracking congressional pork in the nation's capital. Research on swine odor is one of the projects listed in the "Pig Book," released Tuesday. Citizens Against Government Waste is out with its annual "Pig Book" -- a list of lawmakers whom the group considers the most egregious porkers, members of the House and Senate who use the earmarking process to funnel money to projects on their home turf. Fittingly perhaps, the list includes nearly $1.8 million for swine odor and manure management research in Iowa. "In fiscal year 2009, Congress stuffed 10,160 projects into the 12 appropriations bills worth $19.6 billion," the group said in a report released Tuesday. The amount marks a 14 percent increase over 2008. The "Pig Book" also names dozens of what it considers the most blatant examples of pork-barrel spending.  See a list of those projects »  "Taxpayers are ready to revolt," said Tom Schatz, the organization's president. "Despite repeated claims by members of Congress that earmarks have been reduced, the Pig Book belies that claim." Included in the funding is $3.8 million for the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy -- a group dedicated to finding a new use for the stadium that the Detroit Tigers baseball team played in from 1896 through 1999. An additional $1.9 million went to the Pleasure Beach water taxi service project in Bridgeport, Connecticut, requested by then-Rep. Chris Shays. A bridge fire more than a decade ago means beach-goers have to travel a couple of extra miles to get to the beach. Alaska led the nation in pork per capita, at $322 a person. At the bottom of the list was Arizona, with less than $12 per resident. Sen. John McCain does not request earmarks for his home state.  See where each state ranks » . Mississippi Sen. The chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Sen. Daniel Inouye, D-Hawaii, was second, with $445 million. Hawaii Reps. Neil Abercrombie and Mazie Hirono, both Democrats, topped the list for earmarks in the House of Representatives. Abercrombie's pet projects received a total of almost $257 million; Hirono's received almost $153 million. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, was granted the organization's so-called "Porkasaurus" award for earmarking $143,000 for the Las Vegas Natural History Museum. "Sen. Reid is fond of saying that earmarks have been around since we were a country. Now he must be blaming it on the dinosaurs," Schatz said. Some recipients of the earmarks disagreed with the characterization of their projects as "pork." Kathleen Wendler, a member of the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy's board of directors, argued that the $3.8 million dedicated to the old ballpark was critical to revitalizing the surrounding Detroit neighborhood. The money "is not pork at all," she said. The ballpark, if properly utilized, can be an "economic development generator for the local business district. This project will help draw younger people into the neighborhood. It will help save the neighborhood in the long run." To qualify for the "Pig Book," a project must meet at least one of these standards: It was requested by only one chamber of Congress; was not specifically authorized; was not competitively awarded; was not requested by the president; greatly exceeded the president's budget request or the previous year's funding; was not the subject of congressional hearings; or served only a local or special interest. -- CNN's Alan Silverleib contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Listen closely, and you may hear squeals of disgust from a watchdog group tracking congressional pork in the nation’s capital.

Research on swine odor is among the projects listed in the annual “Pig Book,” released Tuesday by Citizens Against Government Waste. The publication identifies lawmakers whom the group considers the most egregious porkers—members of the House and Senate who use the earmarking process to direct money to projects in their home districts and states.

Fittingly, perhaps, the list includes nearly $1.8 million for research on swine odor and manure management in Iowa.

“In fiscal year 2009, Congress stuffed 10,160 projects into the 12 appropriations bills worth $19.6 billion,” the group said in a report released Tuesday. The amount represents a 14 percent increase over 2008.

The “Pig Book” also identifies dozens of what the group considers the most blatant examples of pork-barrel spending.

See a list of those projects »

“Taxpayers are ready to revolt,” said Tom Schatz, the organization’s president. “Despite repeated claims by members of Congress that earmarks have been reduced, the Pig Book belies that claim.”

The funding includes $3.8 million for the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy, a group dedicated to finding a new use for the stadium where the Detroit Tigers baseball team played from 1896 through 1999.

An additional $1.9 million went to the Pleasure Beach water taxi service project in Bridgeport, Connecticut, at the request of then-Rep. Chris Shays. Because of a bridge fire more than a decade ago, beachgoers must travel a couple of extra miles to reach the beach.

Alaska led the nation in pork spending per capita, at $322 per person. Arizona ranked last, with less than $12 per resident. Sen. John McCain does not request earmarks for his home state.

See where each state ranks »

Mississippi Sen. Thad Cochran, the ranking Republican on the Senate Appropriations Committee, topped the list of senators receiving earmarks, with a total of $653 million. The committee’s chairman, Sen. Daniel Inouye, D-Hawaii, ranked second, with $445 million.

Hawaii Reps. Neil Abercrombie and Mazie Hirono, both Democrats, topped the House of Representatives’ earmark list. Abercrombie’s pet projects received nearly $257 million, while Hirono’s received almost $153 million.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, received the organization’s so-called “Porkasaurus” award for earmarking $143,000 for the Las Vegas Natural History Museum.

“Sen. Reid is fond of saying that earmarks have been around since we were a country. Now he must be blaming it on the dinosaurs,” Schatz said.

Some earmark recipients disagreed with the characterization of their projects as “pork.”

Kathleen Wendler, a member of the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy’s board of directors, argued that the $3.8 million dedicated to the old ballpark was critical to revitalizing the surrounding Detroit neighborhood.

The funding “is not pork at all,” she said. If properly utilized, the ballpark can be an “economic development generator for the local business district. This project will help draw younger people into the neighborhood. It will help save the neighborhood in the long run.”

To qualify for inclusion in the “Pig Book,” a project must meet at least one of the following criteria: It was requested by only one chamber of Congress; was not specifically authorized; was not competitively awarded; was not requested by the president; greatly exceeded the president’s budget request or the previous year’s funding; was not the subject of congressional hearings; or served only a local or special interest.

— CNN’s Alan Silverleib contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — A government-spending watchdog in the nation’s capital is raising objections to congressional pork-barrel projects—including research into the smell of pigs.

Citizens Against Government Waste released its yearly “Pig Book” on Tuesday. The report identifies House and Senate members whom the organization views as the worst offenders in using earmarks to direct federal funds toward projects in their own states or districts.

Among the expenditures is nearly $1.8 million for research in Iowa on swine odor and manure management.

According to the organization’s report, Congress inserted 10,160 projects, totaling $19.6 billion, into the 12 appropriations bills for fiscal year 2009. That represents a 14 percent rise from 2008.

The publication also highlights dozens of projects the group regards as particularly conspicuous examples of pork-barrel spending. View a list of those projects »

Tom Schatz, president of Citizens Against Government Waste, said taxpayers were on the verge of rebelling. Although members of Congress have repeatedly asserted that earmarks have declined, he said, the findings in the “Pig Book” contradict those statements.

The spending includes $3.8 million for the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy, an organization working to find a new purpose for the former home of the Detroit Tigers. The baseball team played at the stadium from 1896 to 1999.

Another $1.9 million was allocated to the Pleasure Beach water-taxi project in Bridgeport, Connecticut, at the request of then-Rep. Chris Shays. Because a bridge burned more than 10 years earlier, visitors must travel several additional miles to reach the beach.

On a per-person basis, Alaska ranked first in the country for pork spending, at $322 per resident. Arizona placed last, receiving less than $12 per person. Sen. John McCain does not seek earmarks for his home state. View the rankings for every state »

Mississippi Sen. Thad Cochran, the senior Republican on the Senate Appropriations Committee, led all senators in earmarks, receiving a combined $653 million. Sen. Daniel Inouye, the Hawaii Democrat who chaired the committee, ranked second with $445 million.

In the House, Hawaii Democrats Neil Abercrombie and Mazie Hirono occupied the top two positions. Projects associated with Abercrombie received nearly $257 million, while Hirono’s projects obtained almost $153 million.

The organization presented Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, with its so-called “Porkasaurus” award for securing a $143,000 earmark for the Las Vegas Natural History Museum.

Schatz joked that Reid often says earmarks have existed since the country’s founding and suggested that the senator must now be attributing them to dinosaurs.

Some beneficiaries rejected the claim that their funding amounted to pork. Kathleen Wendler, who served on the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy’s board, said the $3.8 million for the former stadium was essential to efforts to revive the surrounding Detroit community.

She insisted the expenditure was not pork, arguing that a properly repurposed stadium could stimulate economic growth in the nearby business district. She also said the project would attract younger residents and ultimately help preserve the neighborhood.

For inclusion in the “Pig Book,” a project must satisfy at least one of several criteria: it was sought by only one chamber of Congress; lacked specific authorization; was awarded without competition; was not requested by the president; substantially surpassed either the president’s proposed budget or the previous year’s funding; received no congressional hearing; or benefited only a local or special interest.

CNN’s Alan Silverleib contributed to the report.

Citizens Against Government Waste used its annual “Congressional Pig Book” to challenge lawmakers’ claims that they were bringing earmark spending under control. The watchdog group’s fiscal 2009 report identified 10,160 projects inserted into federal spending bills at a total cost of $19.6 billion.

Although the number of earmarks declined from the previous year, their overall cost rose by about 14 percent. According to the organization, that increase showed that Congress had not meaningfully reduced pork-barrel spending; instead, lawmakers were directing larger sums toward individual projects while pointing to the lower project count as evidence of reform.

The report highlighted a range of expenditures that Citizens Against Government Waste considered unnecessary, parochial, or unrelated to pressing national priorities. Examples included federal funding for research into swine odor and manure management, the redevelopment of a stadium, and a water taxi service. Such projects, the group argued, may benefit particular communities or political constituencies but should be financed locally or evaluated through the regular competitive budget process rather than added to legislation at the request of individual members of Congress.

The “Pig Book” is intended to draw public attention to earmarks—funds designated by lawmakers for specific recipients or projects, often without open competition or extensive debate. Critics say the practice encourages waste, rewards politically influential districts, and makes it harder to hold federal spending accountable. Supporters counter that elected representatives understand their communities’ needs and should have a role in deciding where federal money is spent.

In the aftermath of the financial crisis, however, the increase to $19.6 billion attracted especially sharp taxpayer criticism. With federal deficits rising and families facing economic uncertainty, watchdogs argued that Congress should apply greater scrutiny to discretionary projects. Citizens Against Government Waste said the fiscal 2009 figures demonstrated that promises of earmark reform had fallen short and that stronger transparency and spending controls were still needed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Citizens Against Government Waste’s 2009 “Pig Book,” highlighting notable congressional earmarks, state rankings, and lawmakers receiving the most funding.
counterfactuals.output:
# Watchdog’s 2009 ‘Pig Book’ spotlights billions in congressional earmarks

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — From swine-odor research in Iowa to astronomy promotion in Hawaii, a taxpayer watchdog group says Congress packed the 2009 federal spending bills with thousands of projects benefiting lawmakers’ home states and districts.

Citizens Against Government Waste said its 2009 *Congressional Pig Book* identified **10,160 earmarks costing $19.6 billion**. Both figures were lower than in the previous year, but the group argued that lawmakers had failed to end the practice of directing federal money to specific projects outside the normal competitive or agency-review process.

Among the earmarks highlighted by the group were:

- **$1.8 million** for research into swine odor and manure management in Iowa;
- **$2 million** to promote astronomy in Hawaii;
- **$1 million** to control Mormon crickets in Utah;
- **$951,500** for a “sustainable Las Vegas” initiative;
- **$190,000** for the Buffalo Bill Historical Center in Wyoming;
- **$95,000** for a proposed mob museum in Las Vegas; and
- **$200,000** for a tattoo-removal program in California.

CAGW also pointed to funding for honeybee research, grape genetics and other agricultural programs that it said should have competed through regular federal grant channels.

The organization ranked states both by total earmark funding and by spending per resident. Large states, including **California**, were among the leaders in overall dollars, while smaller states with powerful appropriators dominated the per-capita list. **Hawaii, Alaska and Mississippi** ranked near the top in earmark dollars per resident, reflecting major defense, transportation and research projects secured by their congressional delegations.

Mississippi’s senators were among the biggest recipients of earmark credit. According to CAGW’s accounting, Republican **Sen. Thad Cochran**, then the ranking member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, was associated with roughly **$470 million** in earmarks, the highest total for an individual lawmaker. Fellow Mississippi Republican **Sen. Roger Wicker** was credited with about **$390 million**.

The totals can overlap because several lawmakers may sponsor the same project, and CAGW’s methodology counts funding associated with jointly requested earmarks. For that reason, individual lawmakers’ totals should not be added together to calculate overall spending.

Supporters of earmarks have long argued that members of Congress know their states and districts better than federal agencies and that publicly disclosed projects can meet legitimate local needs. Critics counter that the process rewards political influence, bypasses competition and encourages spending on projects with limited national value.

CAGW said the 2009 total represented a decline from fiscal 2008, when it counted 11,610 projects worth $22.1 billion. Still, the group said the nearly $20 billion identified in the latest report showed that congressional promises to curb pork-barrel spending had produced only limited change.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the release of the annual Pig Book and explain why projects such as Iowa swine-odor research, Detroit’s Old Tiger Stadium, and a Connecticut water taxi were labeled pork-barrel spending.
counterfactuals.output:
The watchdog group Citizens Against Government Waste (CAGW) highlighted those projects in its **2009 Congressional Pig Book**, released in spring 2009. The report identified **10,160 earmarked projects costing about $19.6 billion**—fewer projects than in 2008, but roughly 14 percent more money.

Among the examples it publicized were approximately:

- **$1.8 million for swine-odor and manure-management research in Iowa**
- **$3.8 million connected with preserving or redeveloping Detroit’s former Tiger Stadium**
- **$1.9 million for a water-taxi project in Connecticut**

CAGW called them “pork” not necessarily because the projects had no conceivable value, but because they were **congressionally directed expenditures with narrow local or special-interest benefits**. Its Pig Book generally includes spending that meets at least one criterion such as being:

- inserted by Congress rather than requested by the president;
- not competitively awarded;
- not specifically authorized or fully examined in hearings;
- directed to a particular location or recipient; or
- of primarily local rather than national benefit.

Thus, the Iowa research was portrayed as a locally directed agricultural earmark rather than competitively selected federal research; Tiger Stadium was viewed as a local redevelopment or preservation responsibility; and the Connecticut water taxi chiefly served a particular community’s transportation or recreational needs.

Supporters argued that such appropriations could support useful research, economic redevelopment, jobs, and transportation. The Pig Book’s point, however, was that those merits should be tested through normal authorization, review, and competitive funding processes rather than secured through individual lawmakers’ earmarks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed news story about congressional earmarks in fiscal year 2009, including the total number and value of projects, reactions from taxpayer watchdog Tom Schatz, and defenses from earmark recipients.
counterfactuals.output:
**Watchdog counts 10,160 congressional earmarks worth $19.6 billion in fiscal 2009**

**WASHINGTON —** Congress approved 10,160 earmarked projects costing $19.6 billion in fiscal year 2009, according to Citizens Against Government Waste, renewing a long-running dispute over whether lawmakers were directing federal money to legitimate local needs or using public funds to reward favored constituencies.

The watchdog group’s annual *Congressional Pig Book* found that the number of projects fell 12.5 percent from 11,610 in fiscal 2008. Their total cost, however, increased about 14 percent from the previous year’s $17.2 billion.

The tally covered earmarks across the fiscal 2009 appropriations bills, including money for military research, universities, museums, agricultural programs, transportation projects and local economic-development initiatives. It was broader than some other counts because Citizens Against Government Waste applied its own criteria to identify spending it considered improperly directed, including projects requested by only one chamber of Congress, added outside normal competitive procedures or serving a narrow local interest.

Tom Schatz, president of Citizens Against Government Waste, said the figures showed that Congress had not fulfilled promises to reform the earmarking process. Although lawmakers had adopted disclosure rules and reduced the raw number of projects, Schatz argued that the rise in their overall cost demonstrated that earmarking remained deeply embedded in the appropriations system.

Schatz also objected to lawmakers’ practice of describing earmarks as a small part of the federal budget. At a time of recession, deficits and large federal rescue programs, he said, Congress should be applying greater scrutiny to every expenditure rather than treating locally directed projects as insignificant.

The watchdog highlighted projects with unusual-sounding titles, including research involving livestock waste and odor, grape genetics, insect control and specialized local facilities. Such items, Schatz said, often avoided the competitive review that federal agencies normally use to determine scientific or economic merit.

Recipients and sponsoring lawmakers countered that colorful descriptions could make serious work sound frivolous. Agricultural researchers, for example, said studies of animal waste and odor addressed water quality, public health and conflicts between large livestock operations and nearby communities. Supporters of crop and grape research said federally backed work could help farmers resist disease, improve yields and sustain regional agricultural industries.

Universities and nonprofit organizations likewise defended earmarked grants as investments in research, education and employment. They argued that smaller institutions and regional projects might struggle to compete in national grant programs even when they addressed pressing local problems. Community groups said federal support often supplied only part of a project’s budget and could attract matching money from state, local or private sources.

Lawmakers who requested the money also rejected the suggestion that federal agencies should make all spending decisions. They said members of Congress were elected to identify the needs of their districts and that appropriations were a constitutional legislative responsibility. Under that view, a publicly disclosed earmark for a bridge, laboratory or community program was more accountable than an agency grant awarded by unelected officials.

Critics responded that disclosure did not solve the central problem: earmarks could be inserted into large spending bills without hearings, competitive bidding or an up-or-down vote on the individual project. They also warned that even worthy projects could be used to build support for costly appropriations legislation.

The $19.6 billion figure should not be confused with narrower estimates of the earmarks contained only in the large fiscal 2009 omnibus spending package. Other organizations, using different definitions, reported lower totals. The variation reflected disagreements over what qualified as an earmark—for example, whether to include administration-supported projects, spending listed only in committee reports, or programs benefiting a limited number of locations.

Still, the Citizens Against Government Waste report provided fresh ammunition to lawmakers seeking a moratorium or stricter limits. It also underscored the core divide in the earmark debate: taxpayer groups saw politically directed spending with inadequate oversight, while recipients saw federal support for projects that could produce tangible scientific, economic and community benefits.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the findings of the 2009 Citizens Against Government Waste report, naming the top states and members of Congress for earmark spending and explaining the criteria used to classify a project as pork.
counterfactuals.output:
Citizens Against Government Waste’s **2009 Congressional Pig Book** identified:

- **10,160 earmarked projects**
- **$19.6 billion in spending**
- About **12.5% fewer projects than in 2008**, but roughly **14% more money**

### Leading states and lawmakers

On CAGW’s preferred **per-capita** measure, the leading states were:

1. **Alaska** — about **$322 per resident**
2. **Hawaii** — about **$225 per resident**
3. **North Dakota** — about **$143 per resident**

Among senators, the largest earmark totals were attributed to:

- **Sen. Thad Cochran, R-Miss.** — roughly **$474 million**
- **Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss.** — roughly **$391 million**
- **Sen. Mary Landrieu, D-La.** — roughly **$332 million**
- **Sen. Tom Harkin, D-Iowa** — roughly **$292 million**
- **Sen. David Vitter, R-La.** — roughly **$249 million**

In the House, **Rep. John Murtha, D-Pa.**, was the leading earmarker, with approximately **$120 million**. Totals could include jointly sponsored earmarks, so they should not always be read as unique spending controlled by one member.

### How CAGW defined “pork”

A project was classified as pork if it met **at least one** of seven criteria:

1. Requested by only one chamber of Congress  
2. Not specifically authorized  
3. Not competitively awarded  
4. Not requested by the president  
5. Greatly exceeded the president’s budget request or the prior year’s funding  
6. Was not the subject of congressional hearings  
7. Served only a local or special interest  

Thus, CAGW’s label did not necessarily mean a project was illegal or useless; it meant the project displayed at least one characteristic the organization associated with nontransparent, parochial, or insufficiently scrutinized spending.

# Watchdog Group Squeals Over Congressional Pork

Congress’s appetite for earmarks showed little sign of shrinking in fiscal 2009, according to Citizens Against Government Waste, which cataloged 10,160 projects worth $19.6 billion in its annual *Congressional Pig Book*.

The number of projects fell 12.5 percent from the 11,610 identified in fiscal 2008. Their total cost, however, rose roughly 14 percent from $17.2 billion, the watchdog group reported.

“While the number of projects declined, taxpayers paid more for them,” the group said, arguing that lawmakers continued to steer federal money toward projects that had not been requested by the president or subjected to the normal competitive process.

Among the expenditures highlighted in the 2009 report were:

- $1.8 million for swine-odor and manure-management research in Iowa;
- $819,000 for catfish-genetics research in Alabama;
- $1.9 million for a water taxi serving Pleasure Beach in Connecticut;
- $200,000 for a tattoo-removal program in Mission Hills, California; and
- $95,000 for the Montana World Trade Center.

The report’s most prominent dishonor went to Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., who received the group’s “Porkasaurus Award.” Citizens Against Government Waste credited Reid with securing or facilitating roughly $4.2 billion in projects identified as pork—more than any other member of Congress in that year’s book.

The *Pig Book* uses the term “pork” for spending that meets at least one of several criteria, including being requested by only one chamber of Congress, not being competitively awarded, not being requested by the president, or serving a narrow local interest.

Supporters of earmarks dispute the watchdog’s framing. They argue that members of Congress know their states and districts better than federal agencies do and that many locally directed projects support research, transportation, public safety and economic development. Critics counter that even worthwhile projects should compete openly for federal funds rather than depend on the influence of individual lawmakers.

At $19.6 billion, earmarks represented only a small portion of overall federal spending. But the 2009 *Pig Book* argued that the practice symbolized a broader failure of budget discipline—especially because the cost of earmarks rose even as Washington faced mounting deficits.

For taxpayers, the group’s message was simple: Congress may have trimmed the number of trips to the trough, but the remaining servings were larger.
